title: The Luddites: Misunderstood Working Class Heroes
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in the transcript as iHeart Intro/Chuck) examine the Luddites, English textile workers in the Midlands and Yorkshire who broke machines between 1811 and 1813. They cover the pre-industrial hand-loom trade and guild system, the arrival of steam-powered automated looms, the economic and political context (Adam Smith, the Napoleonic War recession, Parliament's refusal to regulate and the 1799 Combination Acts), the mythical leader Ned Lud, the targeted machine-breaking raids (including the Hollingsworth attack and the Battle of Rawfolds Mill), the assassination of William Horsefall, the government's military response and hangings, and the Luddite label's later use. The episode closes with a discussion of Thomas Pynchon's 1984 essay and Brian Merchant's book Blood in the Machine as parallels to modern AI anxieties, followed by a listener mail about Dr. Bronner's soap in gardening.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the episode's article and set up the topic of the Luddites.

segments.title: What the Luddites were
segments.summary: Josh gives a simplified view of the Luddites as textile workers who broke machines; Chuck says they were early workers' rights advocates who turned to machine-breaking only after negotiation failed.

segments.title: The 2012 Olympics and the Industrial Revolution in England
segments.summary: The hosts recall the London 2012 opening ceremony's depiction of industrialization and note that England industrialized before America, with mills concentrated in northern England.

segments.title: Midlands geography and county names
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the counties of the English Midlands and how shire suffixes relate to county seats, using Leicestershire and Leicester as an example.

segments.title: Pre-industrial craft and domestic textile work
segments.summary: Skilled artisans worked through apprenticeships and guilds, weaving at home on hand looms funded by merchants who split profits. William Gardner's account describes a leisurely life, and the hosts contrast it with the sudden shift to 12 to 13 hour factory days.

segments.title: Early automation and William Lee's stocking frame
segments.summary: Automation predated the Luddites; Queen Elizabeth I reportedly refused William Lee a patent in 1589 over job losses. The machines improved over time, and combining them made mills possible.

segments.title: Adam Smith and free-market ideas
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, was used by the merchant class to justify profit maximization, though Smith did not explicitly advocate worker exploitation.

segments.title: Economic recession and incentives to automate
segments.summary: England's wars with Napoleon and blockades closed trade markets, causing recession and hunger. Owners had reason to replace workers with cheaper machines, and the hosts discuss how cheaper, lower-quality goods changed craftsmanship.

segments.title: Quality decline and the origins of capitalism debate
segments.summary: Craftsmen faced a choice between cheaper production or closure. Hosts debate whether capitalism is inherently exploitative or can be made equitable.

segments.title: Break and banter
segments.summary: Short mid-episode break with the hosts joking about a dramatic structure.

segments.title: Workers' demands and Parliament's refusal
segments.summary: Luddites sought fair wages, safe conditions and phased change, but Parliament refused to regulate. Lawmakers argued regulation would hurt business and jobs.

segments.title: Combination Acts and the death penalty for machine-breaking
segments.summary: The 1799 Combination Acts outlawed trade guilds, collective bargaining and strikes, and machine-breaking was made punishable by hanging. The hosts compare this to modern hacking laws.

segments.title: Organization of the Luddites and the myth of Ned Lud
segments.summary: The Luddites were organized and decentralized. Ned Lud is described as a likely fictitious figure, supposedly a weaver who broke his loom in 1779, and a catch-all name for machine breakage.

segments.title: Spread of the Luddite movement and Ned Lud as a fictional leader
segments.summary: The hosts describe the movement's spread from Nottingham and the mythic General Ludd, with authorities believing a real leader existed.

segments.title: First Luddite protest and raid, March 1811
segments.summary: In March 1811 workers protested pay and conditions, troops dispersed them, and they returned that night to trash a mill.

segments.title: Hollingsworth attack
segments.summary: In November 1811 Luddites broke the automatic looms of Edward Hollingsworth, whose cheap stockings had undermined the trade; a week later they burned his house down.

segments.title: Targeted raids and warning letters
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Luddite raids were targeted at abusive employers, that warning letters were sent, and that they intercepted machinery being moved at night.

segments.title: Digression and loom-breaking rate
segments.summary: Brief tangent about Beetlejuice, followed by the estimate that Luddites broke about 175 looms a month.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the escalation in 1812.

segments.title: 1812 escalation and the Battle of Rawfolds Mill
segments.summary: Violence escalated in 1812. The Battle of Rawfolds Mill in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, saw 100 to 200 former workers storm the mill, with armed guards and a gun battle.

segments.title: Assassination of William Horsefall
segments.summary: Horsefall, an outspoken anti-Luddite mill owner, was shot and died days later after the Luddites took him back to the bar where he had been drinking. The hosts note he had bought drinks for workers that night.

segments.title: Community secrecy and government spies
segments.summary: Local communities protected the Luddites, and government spies failed to infiltrate the movement.

segments.title: Military deployment and public hangings
segments.summary: The government deployed about 14,000 troops, more than it had in the Napoleonic War, and hanged dozens of Luddites after hasty trials, including teenagers. Some were transported to Australia.

segments.title: Repeal of union ban and the Luddite reputation
segments.summary: Parliament repealed the ban on unions in 1824. The hosts say the popular anti-technology image of Luddites came from C.P. Snow and was reinforced in the 1970s.

segments.title: Pynchon, Blood in the Machine, and modern AI
segments.summary: Thomas Pynchon's 1984 essay 'Is it OK to be a Luddite?' urged caution about technology. Brian Merchant's book Blood in the Machine draws parallels to AI and job losses, and the hosts note that people questioning AI are labeled Luddites.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail about Dr. Bronner's
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, then read a listener email from Cash, a Portland, Maine gardener who uses diluted Dr. Bronner's soap as an insecticidal spray.
